title: Box Packing
prompt: You have 53 bricks, each with dimensions 1×1×4. You also have a 6×6×6 box. The total volume of the bricks (212) is less than the volume of the box (216).
Can you pack all 53 bricks into the box?
hints: Volume alone doesn't determine whether a packing is possible. Think about structure, not just totals.
Imagine dividing the 6×6×6 box into 27 smaller 2×2×2 sub-cubes. Colour them like a 3D checkerboard — alternating black and white.
Any 1×1×4 brick placed in the box must pass through exactly two 2×2×2 sub-cubes — one black and one white. How many bricks can fit given 13 sub-cubes of one colour?
solution_lede:
Volume is a necessary condition for packing, not a sufficient one. The key is a 3D colouring argument — the same idea that proves you can't tile a mutilated chessboard.

Imagine the 6×6×6 box as 27 smaller 2×2×2 sub-cubes, coloured like a 3D checkerboard: alternating black and white. This gives either 14 black and 13 white, or 13 black and 14 white.

Now consider how a 1×1×4 brick sits in the box. Regardless of orientation, it must occupy exactly two consecutive 2×2×2 sub-cubes — one black and one white. Each 2×2×2 sub-cube can accommodate at most 4 such bricks (one per unit-wide lane through it).

The colour with only 13 sub-cubes can support at most 13 × 4 = 52 bricks. There is no room for the 53rd. Packing is impossible.

solution_steps.body: Divide the 6×6×6 box into 27 sub-cubes of size 2×2×2. Colour them like a 3D checkerboard: 14 of one colour, 13 of the other.
Every 1×1×4 brick, regardless of orientation, spans exactly two adjacent 2×2×2 sub-cubes — one of each colour.
Each 2×2×2 sub-cube can be used by at most 4 bricks (one per unit-wide channel through it).
The minority colour has 13 sub-cubes × 4 bricks = 52 bricks maximum. The 53rd brick cannot be placed.
